episodes.title: What Is an Inference Engine, Anyway? — Charles Frye, Modal
episodes.description:
A traffic spike on a museum placard generator produces longer waits for the first token and slower tokens afterward. Charles Frye reads those symptoms from an inference dashboard and shows how additional replicas relieve the queue. The example connects an application people can see to the machinery behind its API. He follows a request through server IO, tokenization, scheduling, model execution, and detokenization, using SGLang and vLLM as reference points. The scheduler controls what reaches the GPU and can become a bottleneck even though it performs far less computation. Chatbots, background agents, and document processors place different demands on that machinery, with latency budgets, input and output lengths, and prefix reuse shaping the deployment.

Frye then opens up the performance techniques inside the engine. KV caching reuses previously computed work, while cache capacity and layout determine how effectively the engine can keep requests moving. CUDA graphs reduce repeated work on the CPU that launches GPU operations. Speculative decoding lets a speculator model propose several tokens for the target model to check together. Kernel libraries handle much of the underlying computation, leaving the engine to organize batches and avoid getting in the GPU's way. The final section turns to correctness and production debugging: evaluate the actual deployment, log token IDs for tokenizer problems, and collect enough metrics and traces to investigate regressions across replicas. Small reference engines provide a starting point for reading the code and asking deeper architectural questions.

episodes.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 201 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
episodes.description:
A toy store agent fails a request for toys under $6 because its search tool has no price filter. Laurie Voss turns that missing feature into a live demonstration of an improvement loop: add observability, inspect what happened, find the problem, and ask a coding agent to fix it. The Wonder Toys application starts without traces flowing into Arize AX. Skills installed in the workshop repository help the coding agent add tracing and query the resulting data. The diagnosis reaches beyond exceptions and HTTP errors to search quality, including empty results and overly narrow filters. After adding price filtering, Voss repeats the shopping request and checks the new input and output in the trace view.

The broader argument is that reading traces individually stops working when an application produces millions of them. Evals compress behavior into scores and explanations, but people can still become the bottleneck when they must interpret every failure. Voss introduces Signal as another layer that groups recurring problems and suggests fixes. In the demonstration, findings can become GitHub issues, evaluation datasets, new evaluators, or proposed pull requests. Audience questions press on deployment, trust, and preventing a fix from breaking behavior that already works. Regression evals provide that check, while Signal itself has tracing and an evaluation suite. The workshop moves from a manually requested repair toward continuous improvement, with definitions of good behavior directing what the automation should change.

episodes.title: From Raw Documents to AI-Ready Data — Leo Platzer & Jeff Koss
episodes.description:
A chatbot pilot on 40 hand-picked files works great. Point it at 80,000 SharePoint documents and it falls apart.

Jeff Koss and Leo Platzer, co-founder and former CTO of Deasy Labs (acquired by Collibra), walk through taking an unstructured-data AI project from stalled POC to production. Using a manufacturer building a legal-ops chatbot over 80,000 SharePoint files, they demo AI-assisted taxonomies and metadata tagging with evidence and confidence scores, sensitive-data detection, and quality checks for duplicates, conflicts and freshness. Data slices refresh on a schedule. Leo then shows why this matters: when 30% of a corpus is stale or duplicated, up to 80% of an agent's retrieved context can be useless, and cleaning it roughly doubled recall in multi-hop RAG evals. He finishes by generating a context file for coding agents with the SDK.

In this talk:
• Why document data quality means duplicates, conflicts and freshness
• AI-assisted taxonomies and metadata tagging with evidence and confidence
• Finding and filtering sensitive data before it reaches a chatbot
• How stale, duplicated data crowds out good context, and what cleaning it does to recall

episodes.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 101 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
episodes.description:
An LLM correctness judge rejects all 13 reports from a financial analysis agent. Laurie Voss examines why: the agent used live web research, while the judge graded from its own knowledge without that research context. Supplying the collected sources to a faithfulness evaluator produces a more useful split of six faithful reports and seven unfaithful ones. The notebook builds the agent with the Claude Agent SDK and instruments it with OpenTelemetry and OpenInference to send traces to Arize AX. Reading those traces exposes failed file writes, missing report content, and excessive web searches. A deterministic ticker check adds a cheap first layer of evaluation.

Voss builds a custom actionability rubric with explicit criteria, tagged inputs, examples, and binary labels. Each evaluator checks one dimension, so a failure identifies what needs attention. Human annotations provide a comparison set for evaluating the judge, with deliberately random demo labels illustrating how to investigate disagreement. The workshop covers held out tests, precision and recall, judge biases, and the distinction between capability and regression evals. Failing traces become datasets, their explanations guide prompt revisions, and controlled experiments compare the changed agent on the same cases. Online evaluations and production monitoring extend that loop to new traffic, with requirements and recurring failure themes directing subsequent coding agent fixes. The central practice is to read actual traces and define success before automating the grading.

episodes.title: The Transcript Looked Fine. The Call Wasn't. — Debugging Voice Agents, Arize
episodes.description:
The transcript says the agent corrected itself. The audio says it refunded the wrong order.

Fuad Ali, senior product manager at Arize AI, shows why voice agents are one of the hardest categories to debug: latency, turn-taking and transcription errors are invisible in a text log. Using a refund call that looks fine in the transcript but had 2.4 seconds of dead air, an interruption and a refund on the wrong order, he shows what you need instead. That means audio, transcript and trace in one session view, OpenInference semantic conventions for real-time audio across providers, and evals that run on the audio itself. He closes with the observe, evaluate, improve loop and agent experiments that test fixes against failed traces.

In this talk:
• Voice failure modes text logs miss: latency, barge-in, mishearing and tone
• Tracing real-time audio with open-source OpenInference conventions
• Audio-native evals for sentiment, latency, interruptions and task success
• Toward self-healing voice agents: monitors, investigation agents and replayed fixes

episodes.title: Research to Reality with Google DeepMind — Paige Bailey, Google DeepMind
episodes.description:
A model running entirely in the browser produces an emoji table ranking the Harry Potter books, and Paige Bailey immediately questions its taste. The response arrives almost instantly, without an API call or data leaving the machine. Bailey uses that demo to introduce Gemma 4, Google DeepMind's open model family, and show what local inference looks like in practice. She describes Apache 2 licensing, models ranging from two billion to 31 billion parameters, and the ability to download, adapt, and finetune them for a company's own projects. The opening also connects DeepMind's research mission to AlphaFold, medical models, robotics, and AI for science, before outlining computer use and managed agents that execute tasks in a Linux sandbox.

The same local approach extends to phones through Google AI Edge Gallery. Bailey walks through image descriptions, audio transcription, function calling, and a collection of skills for games, haikus, weather queries, and calendar events. Android and iOS devices can run downloaded models, while supported hardware accelerators handle inference instead of relying on the CPU. She then compares model size with deployment requirements: smaller GPU footprints, a single commodity GPU rather than distributed inference, laptop models, and a mobile option. Quantized checkpoints explain the speed of the browser demo, with the two billion parameter version taking less than a gigabyte. The practical thread is choosing a model that fits the device and keeping the work local.

episodes.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 2) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
episodes.description:
A request for facial recognition becomes a job statement about getting attendees into a workshop without missing the first 20 minutes. Kent C. Dodds uses that audience suggestion to separate a requested feature from the progress a user actually needs. Asking why exposes alternatives such as parallel queues or badges, rather than immediately committing to a database of faces. He breaks the job into functional, social, and emotional dimensions, showing how each changes engineering decisions. A system can move people through a door faster while making them uncomfortable about how their information is used. Success also includes whether customers keep using the product, rather than simply paying for it once.

The second exercise shifts to a food delivery app and uses the Kano model to sort competing requests. Reliable order confirmations are basic needs. Delivery estimates offer a measurable performance gradient. Discounts and group ordering can delight users, while GPS tracking illustrates how an unexpected extra becomes something customers assume will exist. Dodds connects those categories to architectural effort: make foundations reliable, measure performance, and keep experiments reversible until their value is clearer. Features that nobody cares about create maintenance work; features users actively dislike deserve pushback. Audience questions cover validating ideas before metrics exist, handling an unusually demanding customer, and understanding architecture during incidents. The closing argument ties technical expertise to product judgment: faster implementation matters when engineers understand which problems deserve solving.

episodes.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 1) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
episodes.description:
The line of attendees waiting outside becomes the workshop's live product idea: an app called Just Get In the Workshop. Kent C. Dodds uses that immediate frustration to practice deciding whether a problem deserves a software solution. Before the exercise, he explains why faster implementation changes the value of an engineer's work. Agents can help hit more targets, but choosing the useful target still requires judgment. Product engineers connect customer needs to data models, workflows, constraints, observability, and the smallest useful slice of a system. Dodds draws on conversations with other builders to show how understanding users changes architectural choices, while accepting a ticket without that context can produce technically polished work that misses the point.

The room then applies The Mom Test to its conference entry idea. Questions about whether somebody would use an app invite compliments and speculation. Questions about the last time the problem happened, what the person did instead, and what the workaround cost reveal behavior. Dodds connects that evidence to how much engineering effort a feature deserves. An experiment needs a different investment from a capability essential to the business. Early prototypes and watching people use them keep the feedback loop open after the initial idea has been validated. Audience questions explore hiring for product judgment, collaboration with product managers, and engineering responsibilities as teams grow. The first part establishes the discovery habits and technical ownership that guide the next stages of the workshop.

episodes.title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Sandbox — Matt Brockman, E2B
episodes.description:
A runaway process consumes 99.7% of a sandbox's CPU, and killing it unlocks the next level of a capture the flag lab. Matt Brockman walks the room through deliberately broken environments to make sandbox operations concrete. Participants identify their sandbox, find memory pressure, locate a file filling the disk, and clean up background processes. Each challenge runs in its own environment, so a mistake can be reset without destroying the rest of the workshop. Brockman explains how E2B templates preserve a running system's state, including memory and the filesystem, so work can resume where it stopped. The exercises begin with Linux commands and configuration before moving into Python.

The operational questions become harder when a few sandboxes turn into hundreds or thousands. A simulated lifecycle exercise gives a task enough time to finish, then shortens the idle timeout so unused resources do not keep consuming capacity. Another exercise replaces round robin assignment with a mapping from users to sandbox IDs, allowing each person to return to the same workspace. A cache example separates a template's readable files from the location that should receive runtime writes. Brockman also discusses the tradeoffs of restoring state: startup is convenient, but forgotten processes come back too. Audience questions cover volumes, storage growth, distributed workloads, orchestration, and network restrictions. The recurring task is keeping track of what runs where, what it can access, and when to clean it up.

episodes.title: Agents That Write Their Own Tools at Runtime — Sandhya Subramani, AWS
episodes.description:
This agent starts with zero tools. Ask it for something it can't do, and it writes the tool and uses it without restarting.

Sandhya Subramani, senior developer advocate for GenAI at AWS, demos meta-tooling with the open-source Strands Agents SDK. That means agents that write, load and use their own tools at runtime, and even spin up their own sub-agents. All it takes is a system prompt describing what a good tool looks like, plus three tools: editor, shell and load_tool. She walks through agentic patterns (swarm, graph, handoff, workflow), demos a travel planner that builds its own sub-agents, and covers the evals and guardrails you need before trusting a self-modifying agent in production.

In this talk:
• Meta-tooling: editor, shell and load_tool plus one system prompt
• Agents that create their own sub-agents
• Evals for self-modifying agents: goal success, tool choice, parameters, inter-agent flow
• Guardrails: sandboxed execution, constrained permissions and observability
